newsitem.title: USA: NYC files class action against U.S. auto insurers.
newsitem.headline: NYC files class action against U.S. auto insurers.

text.p: A lawsuit seeking class-action status was filed on Thursday in state Supreme Court against seven U.S. automobile insurers, claiming they overcharged New Yorkers by failing to pass on the savings generated by a dramatic drop in car thefts.
The suit, filed by the city of New York on behalf of the 500,000 New York city residents who hold comprehensive auto insurance, seeks millions of dollars in compensation.
It also seeks an injunction ordering the insurers to lower automobile comprehensive insurance rates and premiums.

Defendants named in the complaint are Travelers Property Casualty Corp's Aetna Casualty & Surety Co and Travelers Indemnity Co., Allstate Corp's Allstate Insurance Co, Berkshire Hathaway Inc's Government Employees Insurance Co (GEICO), Liberty Mutual Insurance Co, Nationwide Mutual Insurance Co, and State Farm Fire & Casualty Insurance Co
In its lawsuit, the city claimed automobile theft in New York dropped to under 60,000 in 1996 from 145,000 in 1990 and continued to decline in 1997.

"Such a massive reduction in automobile theft should have been accompanied by an equally massive reduction in premiums for the type of insurance which covers such losses, automobile comprehensive insurance," the complaint said.
"This is especially true since automobile theft represents nearly 80 percent of the losses paid under such insurance in New York," the complaint said.
However, insurers have failed to appropriately adjust their insurance rates from 1991 to the present, according to the complaint.

"The defendant insurance companies have consistently failed to adjust their automobile comprehensive insurance rates to adequately reflect the enormous savings generated by this reduction in automobile thefts in New York City," the lawsuit claimed.

But the National Association of Independent Insurers, a non-profit trade group representing more than 565 property-casualty insurance companies, disagreed, saying comprehensive auto insurance rates in New York City have declined along with the city's auto theft rate.
The NAII said State Farm reduced its comprehensive rates in Manhattan 24 percent in 1995 and Nationwide's comprehensive rates fell 21.9 percent in the five boroughs from 1995 to 1996.
GEICO's comprehensive rates fell 19.3 percent from 1988 to 1995 and Allstate's comprehensive rates fell 24 percent on average in the five boroughs since 1991, the NAII said.

"It is important to consider that although theft is a major component of comprehensive coverage, fire, glass, vandalism and weather-related damage all fall under the comprehensive rate as well," said Robert Zeman, vice president and assistant general counsel for NAII.
The price of the policy is driven by a number of factors in addition to comprehensive coverage such as liability coverage over which the industry has little or no control, the NAII said.
In New York City, liability coverage comprises slightly more than half of the total premium cost, Zeman said
Claims for liability losses in New York continue to rise at a rate as high as 58 percent for Brooklyn during 1989-1993, the NAII said.
